config.title: useEffect & Side Effects

intro.title: useEffect & Side Effects
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build a dynamic user profile component that automatically fetches and displays user data when the component loads, and updates the page title based on the selected user. You'll learn about side effects in Angular - operations that interact with the outside world like API calls, DOM manipulation, or timers - and how to manage them properly using lifecycle hooks. The main concepts covered include the ngOnInit lifecycle hook for component initialization, dependency injection for services, and proper cleanup with ngOnDestroy. You'll work with Angular's component lifecycle, HTTP client for data fetching, and reactive programming patterns using RxJS observables. By the end, you'll understand when and how to perform side effects in Angular components while avoiding common pitfalls like memory leaks.
intro.usecase: Side effects with useEffect are essential in modern web applications for handling data fetching, subscriptions, and cleanup operations. You'll find this pattern in e-commerce sites that fetch product data when components mount, social media feeds that subscribe to real-time updates, and dashboard applications that poll APIs for live metrics. Dating apps use useEffect to track user location changes, streaming platforms manage video player lifecycle events, and banking apps handle authentication token refreshes. Every time you see a loading spinner, auto-updating content, or real-time notifications in apps like Slack, Twitter, or Airbnb, useEffect is managing those side effects behind the scenes.

objectives: Implement useEffect hooks to execute side effects in Angular components
Configure useEffect with dependency arrays to control when effects run
Construct cleanup functions to prevent memory leaks and cancel subscriptions
Apply useEffect to fetch data from external APIs on component mount
Manipulate DOM elements directly using useEffect for imperative operations
Initialize event listeners and timers within useEffect hooks
Integrate multiple useEffect hooks within a single component for different concerns
Control component lifecycle behaviors by binding effects to specific state changes

steps.title: Import Angular Core and OnInit lifecycle hook
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in Component and OnInit from the Angular core library. Both symbols should be imported in a single import statement.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing multiple symbols from a module
import { Router, ActivatedRoute } from '@angular/router';
steps.expectedOutcome: Angular Component decorator and OnInit lifecycle hook are imported and ready to use
successCriteria: Component and OnInit are imported from '@angular/core'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're importing both Component and OnInit from '@angular/core' in a single import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the import statement with curly braces to import Component and OnInit from '@angular/core'.

steps.title: Create the main component class
steps.instruction: Create a component class named EffectDemoComponent that implements the OnInit interface
steps.hint: Use the class keyword followed by the component name, then add 'implements OnInit' to indicate it will use the ngOnInit lifecycle method

seedCode.App.tsx:
// Import Angular core dependencies here

// Create your component class here

steps.expectedOutcome: A component class is created that implements the OnInit interface, preparing it to use Angular's lifecycle hooks
successCriteria: Component class named EffectDemoComponent is created and implements OnInit interface
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your component class implements the OnInit interface so it can use lifecycle methods.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a class that implements OnInit. This interface tells Angular that your component will use the ngOnInit lifecycle method.

steps.title: Initialize component properties for data storage
steps.instruction: Add three properties to your component class: userData to store user information (initialize as null), isLoading to track loading state (initialize as false), and errorMessage to store error messages (initialize as empty string).
steps.hint: In Angular, component properties are declared inside the class body. You can initialize them with default values using the assignment operator.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have three properties to manage different types of data and state throughout the component lifecycle.
successCriteria: Component has userData property initialized as null, isLoading property initialized as false, and errorMessage property initialized as empty string
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure all three properties are present: userData (null), isLoading (false), and errorMessage (empty string).
steps.feedbackWrong: The properties need to be declared inside the component class with proper initialization. Check that you have userData, isLoading, and errorMessage with their correct initial values.

steps.title: Add the ngOnInit lifecycle method
steps.instruction: Add the ngOnInit method to your component class to handle component initialization logic
steps.hint: The ngOnInit method is called after the component's data-bound properties have been initialized. It should be a public method that returns void.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class will have an ngOnInit method ready to handle initialization logic
successCriteria: The ngOnInit method is added to the SideEffectsComponent class
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the ngOnInit method is properly defined within the component class.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ngOnInit method needs to be added to the component class. Remember, it's a lifecycle method that Angular calls during component initialization.

steps.title: Create a data fetching method
steps.instruction: Create a method named 'fetchUserData' that simulates fetching user data by setting a timeout and updating the userData property
steps.hint: Define a method that uses setTimeout to simulate an API call and assigns mock user data to the userData property after a delay
steps.expectedOutcome: A method called fetchUserData that uses setTimeout to simulate asynchronous data fetching and updates the userData property
successCriteria: fetchUserData method is defined and uses setTimeout to update userData property with mock data
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your method uses setTimeout to simulate the async operation and updates the userData property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method should be named 'fetchUserData' and use setTimeout to simulate fetching data by updating the userData property.

steps.title: Call the data fetching method in ngOnInit
steps.instruction: Inside the ngOnInit lifecycle method, call the fetchUserData method to load initial data when the component initializes.
steps.hint: Use `this.fetchUserData()` to invoke the method inside ngOnInit. This ensures data is fetched when the component first loads.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchUserData method is called inside ngOnInit, ensuring data fetching happens when the component initializes.
successCriteria: The ngOnInit method contains a call to this.fetchUserData()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're calling the method with the correct syntax: this.fetchUserData()
steps.feedbackWrong: call the fetchUserData method inside ngOnInit using this.fetchUserData(). This will execute the side effect when the component loads.

steps.title: Create the component template structure
steps.instruction: Replace the existing template with a structured div containing three sections: a loading indicator, an error message display, and a user data display area.
steps.hint: Use Angular template syntax to create conditional sections that will display different states of your component data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now contains a structured div with sections for loading state, error messages, and user data display.
successCriteria: Template contains a main div with nested divs for loading, error, and user data sections using Angular template syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure to include sections for loading, error, and data display within the main container.
steps.feedbackWrong: The template should contain a main div with nested sections for loading, error, and user data display areas.

steps.title: Display loading state in the template
steps.instruction: Add a div with loading message that only displays when isLoading is true using the *ngIf directive
steps.hint: Use *ngIf="isLoading" on a div element to conditionally show the loading message
steps.expectedOutcome: A div with loading message appears in the template that will only show when isLoading is true
successCriteria: Template contains a div with *ngIf="isLoading" and displays a loading message
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure to use *ngIf="isLoading" to conditionally display the loading message.
steps.feedbackWrong: use the *ngIf directive with the isLoading property to conditionally show the loading message.

steps.title: Display fetched data in the template
steps.instruction: Add a div below the loading div to display the user data when it's available using Angular interpolation
steps.hint: Use *ngIf to conditionally show the user data only when userData is not null, and display properties like userData.name using double curly braces
steps.expectedOutcome: A div with conditional rendering that displays user data properties when userData is available
successCriteria: Template includes a div with *ngIf="userData" that displays user data properties using interpolation
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure to use *ngIf to conditionally render the user data and display the properties with double curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: add a div with *ngIf="userData" to conditionally show the data, and use interpolation with {{}} to display the user properties.

steps.title: Display error messages in the template
steps.instruction: Add an error message div that conditionally displays when there's an error using the *ngIf directive.
steps.hint: Use *ngIf="error" to show the div only when the error property has a value, and display the error message inside the div.
steps.expectedOutcome: A div element that conditionally renders error messages when the error property contains a value.
successCriteria: Error message div is added with *ngIf directive that checks the error property and displays the error message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure the div uses *ngIf to conditionally display based on the error property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error display should use *ngIf="error" to conditionally show the div and {{ error }} to display the message.

steps.title: Add a refresh button with click handler
steps.instruction: Add a refresh button to the template that calls the fetchUserData method when clicked
steps.hint: Use the (click) event binding to connect the button to the fetchUserData method
steps.expectedOutcome: A button element is added to the template with a click event binding that calls the fetchUserData method
successCriteria: Template contains a button element with (click) event binding that calls fetchUserData
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your button has the (click) event binding that calls the fetchUserData method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs a (click) event binding. Use (click)="fetchUserData()" to call the method when the button is clicked.

steps.instruction: Run the application to observe the component's lifecycle behavior and verify that the ngOnInit method executes when the component initializes.
